tagline: A herdsman from Judah walks into the prosperous northern kingdom of Israel and announces that God will judge a nation that worships loudly while crushing the poor.
overview:
Amos is usually counted the earliest of the prophets whose words were gathered into a book of their own, and it may be the most direct. Around the middle of the eighth century BC, a man from the village of Tekoa in Judah traveled north to the kingdom of Israel, which was enjoying its greatest wealth in generations under King Jeroboam II. The shrines at Bethel and Gilgal were crowded with worshipers, and the rich had built winter houses, summer houses, and homes decorated with ivory. Amos looked beneath the prosperity and saw courts that took bribes, creditors who sold debtors for the price of a pair of sandals, merchants who rigged their scales, and worship that God refused to accept.

The book opens with a series of judgments on Israel's neighbors for their war crimes, then springs its trap by turning the same judgment on Judah and, at greatest length, on Israel. Chapters 3 to 6 press the charges in sermons, laments, and woes. Chapters 7 to 9 record five visions of coming judgment and a clash with Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, who tells Amos to go home. The book ends with a promise that God will raise up the fallen house of David and restore his people.

Amos matters because he refuses to separate the worship of God from the treatment of neighbors. His line "let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (Amos 5:24) has been quoted for centuries by people who wanted faith to show itself in public life. He also teaches that privilege before God brings accountability rather than immunity, and that the Day of the LORD is not good news for those who assume they are safe.
author:
The book presents itself as "the words of Amos, who was among the sheepherders of Tekoa" (Amos 1:1). In 7:14-15 Amos says he was not a professional prophet or a member of a prophetic guild but a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees whom the LORD took from following the flock. The word used for sheepherder in 1:1 is used elsewhere of King Mesha of Moab, who paid tribute in sheep (2 Kings 3:4), so some scholars think Amos was a substantial owner or manager of flocks rather than a poor hired hand; others think he was a working shepherd. Either way he was a layman from Judah speaking in the north.

Most scholars accept that the core of the book comes from Amos himself, whose oracles were collected and arranged by him or by those who preserved his words. Many critical scholars regard certain passages as later additions: the oracle against Judah (2:4-5), the hymn-like doxologies praising God as creator (4:13; 5:8-9; 9:5-6), and the closing promise of restoration (9:11-15). Other scholars argue that each of these fits Amos's own setting and that the hopeful ending is the natural completion of a message of judgment. The book as it stands has been read as a unity by Jewish and Christian readers throughout their history.
date:
The superscription dates Amos's preaching to the reigns of Uzziah king of Judah (about 792 to 740 BC) and Jeroboam II king of Israel (about 793 to 753 BC), and more precisely to "two years before the earthquake" (1:1). Exact dates for these kings vary by a few years among scholars because of overlapping co-regencies. Most place Amos's ministry around 760 BC, and it may have been brief, perhaps a single season or a single year.

The earthquake was remembered long afterward; Zechariah 14:5 still refers to people fleeing "from the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah". Excavators at Hazor in the north of Israel, and at several other sites in the region, have reported damage layers from a strong earthquake that they date to roughly the middle of the eighth century BC. Linking these directly to the earthquake of Amos 1:1 is reasonable and widely suggested, but archaeological dating is approximate, and the connection remains probable rather than certain. The book was likely written down not long after Amos's preaching, with debate, as noted above, about whether some passages were added later.
setting:
The first half of the eighth century was a season of unusual peace and expansion for Israel and Judah. Assyria, the great power of Mesopotamia, was for several decades preoccupied with internal troubles and other enemies, and Aram (Syria), Israel's northern rival, had been weakened. Jeroboam II took advantage of this and extended Israel's borders to the north and east (2 Kings 14:25), while Uzziah did the same for Judah. Trade flourished, and a class of wealthy landowners and officials grew in Samaria, the capital. Excavations at Samaria recovered carved ivory inlays from this general period, and inscribed potsherds (the Samaria ostraca) recording deliveries of wine and oil to the capital, which help modern readers picture the world Amos describes.

The prosperity was unevenly shared. Small farmers could fall into debt after a bad harvest, lose their land, and be sold into servitude; courts that met in the city gate could be bought. Worship flourished at royal shrines such as Bethel, where Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf generations earlier, and at Gilgal and Beersheba. Within a few years of Jeroboam II's death, Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III (who came to the throne in 745 BC) returned to the west, and in 722 BC Samaria fell and the northern kingdom came to an end. Amos's warnings came about a generation before that collapse.
purpose: Amos was sent to announce to Israel that its end was near and to explain why. The reasons were concrete: oppression of the poor and weak, corruption in the courts, sexual abuse, luxurious living funded by injustice, and a religion that multiplied sacrifices and songs while ignoring what God had commanded. He also called the people to "Seek the LORD and live" (Amos 5:6), leaving open the possibility that God might be gracious to a remnant. The book was preserved so that Judah, and every later community of God's people, could learn from Israel's fall and recognize that God's covenant love includes his demand for justice.
story: Amos stands at the beginning of the great era of the writing prophets, just before Hosea in the north and Isaiah and Micah in the south. The story behind him is the history told in 1 and 2 Kings: the division of Solomon's kingdom, the northern kings' rival shrines at Bethel and Dan, and centuries of prophetic warnings from figures such as Elijah and Elisha. Amos appeals constantly to the exodus, the wilderness years, and the gift of the land, and his social charges echo the laws of the covenant about debt, pledges, fair weights, and justice in court. After him, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC confirmed his words, and his closing promise of a restored house of David points forward to the hope carried by the later prophets and fulfilled, in the New Testament's reading, in Jesus.
christ: Amos's final chapter promises that God will "restore the fallen tent of David" (Amos 9:11). At the Jerusalem council in Acts 15, James quoted this passage, following the wording of the Greek translation of the Old Testament, to show that the inclusion of Gentiles in the church fulfilled what the prophets had said: the risen Christ, David's heir, was rebuilding David's house so that the nations might seek the Lord. Stephen also quoted Amos 5:25-27 in his speech in Acts 7 to show Israel's long history of idolatry. More broadly, Amos's demand that worship and justice belong together is taken up in Jesus's own teaching, as when he rebuked those who tithed garden herbs but neglected justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23). These links are partly direct fulfillment and partly shared conviction, and it is worth keeping the two distinct.
reading: Amos is poetry and prophetic speech, with one short narrative (7:10-17) and a series of visions. Watch for the repeated formula that opens each oracle in chapters 1 and 2, beginning with "For three transgressions of Damascus, even four", the call to "Hear this word" that opens chapters 3, 4, and 5, the refrain "yet you did not return to Me" in chapter 4, and the woes of chapters 5 and 6. Amos uses shocking images (cows of Bashan, a lion's roar, a basket of summer fruit that sounds like the word for the end), and his rhetoric is meant to jolt. Read his social charges for what they name: specific acts of oppression and corruption measured against Israel's covenant law. Readers across the political spectrum have claimed him, but the text itself addresses God's people and their leaders, and its standard is God's covenant, not any modern program. Do not skip the ending; the book closes on restoration.

structure.title: Judgment on the nations, then on Judah and Israel
structure.summary: Eight oracles in the same pattern condemn Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Judah, and finally Israel, whose oppression of the poor receives the longest indictment.

structure.title: Hear this word: privilege and accountability
structure.summary: Because God chose Israel, he will hold it to account. The wealthy of Samaria, the shrines of Bethel, and a people who refused every earlier warning are summoned to meet their God.

structure.title: Lament and woe
structure.summary: A funeral song for fallen Israel, a call to seek the LORD and establish justice, a warning that the Day of the LORD will be darkness, and woes on the complacent rich.

structure.title: Five visions and a confrontation
structure.summary: Visions of locusts, fire, a plumb line, summer fruit, and the Lord at the altar announce judgment, interrupted by Amaziah the priest's order that Amos leave Bethel.

structure.title: The fallen tent of David restored
structure.summary: After judgment, God will raise up the house of David, restore his people's fortunes, and plant them in their land never again to be uprooted.

themes.title: Justice and righteousness
themes.body: Amos pairs two words that run through the whole Old Testament: justice (mishpat), the right ordering of life and especially fair judgment in court, and righteousness (tsedaqah), faithfulness to the obligations of the covenant community. Amos condemns selling the needy, taking bribes, turning away the poor at the gate, and cheating with false weights. For him these are not side issues but the measure of whether a people truly knows God.

themes.title: Worship without obedience
themes.body: Israel's shrines were busy and its offerings generous, but God says he hates their feasts and will not listen to their songs (Amos 5:21-23). Amos does not reject worship as such; he rejects worship that is used as a cover for injustice or as a substitute for obedience. The prophets who followed him, and Jesus after them, made the same point.

themes.title: Election and accountability
themes.body: "Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" (Amos 3:2). Israel assumed that being God's chosen people guaranteed its safety. Amos turns the logic around: those who have received more knowledge of God and more of his gifts will answer for more.

themes.title: God of all nations and all creation
themes.body: Amos's God judges Damascus and Moab for crimes against humanity, brought the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir (9:7), forms the mountains, and names the stars. He is not a tribal deity bound to one land. That universal rule is the ground both for his judgment of Israel and for the hope of a restoration in which the nations bear his name (9:12).

themes.title: The Day of the LORD
themes.body: Israel looked forward to the Day of the LORD as a day of victory over its enemies. Amos, in one of the earliest uses of the phrase in the prophets, warns that it will be darkness and not light for a disobedient people (Amos 5:18-20). The theme recurs throughout the later prophets and into the New Testament.

keyChapters.why: The superscription sets Amos in time and place, and the oracles against the nations show a God who holds every people accountable for cruelty.
The trap closes: after condemning the neighbors, Amos turns on Israel and names its oppression of the poor in concrete detail.
The principle of election and accountability, and the chain of questions that explains why a prophet must speak.
The book's heart: a lament over Israel, the call to seek the LORD and live, the warning about the Day of the LORD, and the demand that justice roll like a river.
Amos's visions and his confrontation with Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, show the prophet's calling and the cost of speaking.
The final vision of judgment gives way to the promise of David's restored tent, quoted by James at the Jerusalem council.

parts.body:
Amos is the third of the twelve shorter prophets, nine chapters long. It is usually counted the earliest of the prophets whose words were gathered into a book of their own, and it may be the most direct. Around 760 BC a man from the village of Tekoa in Judah went north to the kingdom of Israel, which was enjoying its greatest wealth in generations under Jeroboam II.

The shrines at Bethel and Gilgal were crowded, and the rich had winter houses, summer houses and homes decorated with ivory. Amos looked beneath the prosperity. He saw courts that took bribes, creditors who sold the needy ‘for a pair of sandals’ (2:6), merchants who rigged their scales, and worship God refused to accept.

The book opens with judgments on Israel's neighbors for their war crimes, then springs its trap by turning the same judgment on Judah and, at greatest length, on Israel. Chapters 3 to 6 press the charges. Chapters 7 to 9 record five visions and a clash with Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, who tells Amos to go home.

Its best-known line is a call God gives in the middle of his refusal of Israel's feasts: ‘But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream’ (5:24). The book ends with a promise that God will raise up the fallen house of David.

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Amos stands at the beginning of the age of the writing prophets, just before Hosea in the north and Isaiah and Micah in the south. The story behind him is told in 1 and 2 Kings: the division of Solomon's kingdom, the northern kings' rival shrines at Bethel and Dan, and centuries of warnings from prophets such as Elijah and Elisha.

Amos appeals again and again to the exodus, the wilderness years and the gift of the land, and his charges echo the covenant laws about debt, pledges, fair weights and justice in court. About a generation after he spoke, the fall of Samaria confirmed his words. His closing promise of a restored house of David points forward to the hope of the later prophets.

The book calls itself ‘These are the words of Amos, who was among the sheepherders of Tekoa’ (1:1). Later Amos says he was not a prophet by trade, nor a prophet's son, but ‘a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees’ (7:14), whom the LORD took from following the flock. The word for sheepherder in 1:1 is used of King Mesha of Moab, who paid tribute in sheep, so some scholars think Amos owned or managed large flocks; others think he was a working shepherd. Either way, he was a layman from Judah speaking in the north.

Most scholars accept that the core of the book comes from Amos, whose words were collected by him or by those who kept them. Many critical scholars regard some passages as later additions: the word against Judah (2:4-5), the hymns praising God as creator (4:13; 5:8-9; 9:5-6), and the closing promise (9:11-15). Others argue that each fits Amos's own setting and that the hopeful ending completes a message of judgment. Jewish and Christian readers have read the book as one whole throughout their history.

The heading dates Amos to the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel, ‘two years before the earthquake’ (1:1). The site's guide to the kings gives Jeroboam II 793/792 to 753 BC and puts Amos about 760. His preaching may have been brief, a single season or a single year. The earthquake was long remembered (Zechariah 14:5). The guide says archaeologists have identified its traces at Hazor and other sites around 760. The book's introduction is more careful: damage layers at Hazor and other sites date to roughly the middle of the eighth century, and linking them to Amos's earthquake is probable but not certain, since archaeological dating is approximate.

parts.h: Wealth in Samaria, and the poor at the gate
parts.body:
The first half of the eighth century was a season of unusual peace and expansion for Israel and Judah. Assyria was busy with troubles of its own for several decades, and Aram, Israel's northern rival, had been weakened. Jeroboam II pushed Israel's borders north and east, and Uzziah did the same for Judah. Trade flourished, and a class of wealthy landowners and officials grew in Samaria. Excavations there found carved ivory inlays from this general period, and inscribed potsherds, the Samaria ostraca, recording deliveries of wine and oil to the capital.

The wealth was not shared. Small farmers could fall into debt after a bad harvest, lose their land and be sold into servitude, and the courts that met in the city gate could be bought. Worship flourished at royal shrines like Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba. Within a few years of Jeroboam's death, Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III, who came to the throne in 745 BC, returned to the west, and in 722 BC Samaria fell.

The book moves in three parts. Chapters 1 and 2 are a ring of judgments on the nations around Israel, each beginning ‘For three transgressions of Damascus, even four’ (1:3), with the name changed each time, closing in on Judah and then on Israel. Chapters 3 to 6 are sermons, laments and woes, three of them opening with the call to hear this word (3:1; 4:1; 5:1). Chapters 7 to 9 are five visions, interrupted by the one story in the book, Amos and Amaziah at Bethel (7:10-17), and ending with the promise of restoration.

Amos is poetry and prophetic speech. His pictures are meant to jolt: a lion's roar, the cows of Bashan, a basket of summer fruit that sounds like the word for the end. Listen for the refrain of chapter 4, that the people did not return to God, which comes five times (4:6-11).

The LORD roars from Zion (1:2), and the judgments begin. Damascus threshed Gilead with iron. Gaza and Tyre sold whole populations into slavery, and Tyre broke a covenant of brotherhood. Edom pursued its brother with the sword. Ammon committed a war crime against the pregnant women of Gilead to seize land. Moab burned the bones of Edom's king. These notes name these crimes and do not describe them.

None of these nations had received the law at Sinai, and God judges them anyway, for cruelty that every people knows is wrong. A first hearer in Israel would have agreed with every word. Then the trap closes. Judah is judged for rejecting the law of the LORD (2:4). And Israel is judged at the greatest length of all: ‘they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals’ (2:6). They trample the poor, push the needy aside, abuse a young woman, and lie down at their altars on garments taken as pledges from the poor.

God reminds them what he did: he brought them out of Egypt, led them forty years in the wilderness, and raised up prophets and Nazirites. They made the Nazirites drink wine and told the prophets not to prophesy. No one will escape, not the swift, not the strong, not the bravest warrior (2:13-16).

Chapter 3 opens with one of the sharpest sentences in the prophets. ‘Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities’ (3:2). Being chosen did not make Israel safe. It made Israel answerable. A chain of questions follows, each about cause and effect, and ends with the prophet's own: ‘The Lord GOD has spoken’, so who can keep from prophesying (3:8)?

Chapter 4 calls the wealthy women of Samaria ‘cows of Bashan’ (4:1), well-fed cattle from the rich pastures east of the Jordan, who oppress the poor and tell their husbands to bring them drinks. The book's notes say plainly that the image is harsh and that it is aimed at the women's oppression of the poor, not at women as such; Amos is just as hard on the men. Then Amos mocks the busy worship at Bethel and Gilgal, and God lists the warnings he has already sent: famine, drought, blight, locusts, plague, war. Each ends with the refrain that they did not return to God (4:6-11). So ‘prepare to meet your God’ (4:12).

parts.h: Seek the LORD and live, and let justice roll
parts.body:
Chapter 5 begins with a funeral song for Israel, as if the nation were already dead. Then it calls, ‘Seek Me and live’ (5:4), and not the shrines of Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba. Amos condemns those who turn justice into bitterness, take bribes, and silence honest witnesses in the city gate, where courts met. ‘Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate. Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph’ (5:15).

The people longed for the Day of the LORD as a day of victory. Amos warns, ‘It will be darkness and not light’ (5:18). Then God speaks of their worship in some of the hardest words in the Bible: he hates their feasts and will not accept their offerings or listen to their songs. ‘But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream’ (5:24).

Amos does not reject worship as such. The prophets attack sacrifice cut off from obedience, the same point Samuel made to Saul. Chapter 6 adds the woe on those ‘at ease in Zion’ (6:1), who lie on ivory beds, drink wine by the bowlful, ‘but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph’ (6:6). Their sin is not music or feasting but comfort that does not grieve.

Readers across the political spectrum have claimed Amos. The book itself speaks to God's people and their leaders, and its standard is God's covenant, not any modern program.

parts.h: Five visions, and a priest at Bethel
parts.body:
Chapters 7 to 9 record five visions. In the first God shows Amos locusts, and in the second a fire consuming the land. Each time Amos pleads for Jacob, so small, and each time the LORD relents (7:1-6). In the third God shows a plumb line, a weight on a cord used to see whether a wall is straight. Israel is out of true, and God says, ‘I will no longer spare them’ (7:8).

Between the visions comes the only story in the book. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reports Amos to King Jeroboam and tells him to go back to Judah and earn his bread there, because Bethel is the king's sanctuary (7:10-13). Amos answers that he was a herdsman whom the LORD took from following the flock, and he speaks judgment on Amaziah's house.

In the fourth vision Amos sees a basket of summer fruit. In Hebrew the word for summer fruit, qayits, sounds like the word for end, qets, and God says, ‘The end has come for My people Israel’ (8:2). Merchants who cannot wait for the Sabbath to end so they can cheat again (8:4-6) will see a famine, ‘not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD’ (8:11). In the fifth vision Amos sees the Lord beside the altar, and no one can hide from him (9:1-4).

The last chapter reminds Israel that God rules every nation's history: he brought Israel up from Egypt, and the Philistines and the Arameans from their lands too (9:7). The sinful kingdom will be destroyed, but not utterly (9:8).

Then the book turns to hope. ‘In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David’ (9:11). God will repair its ruins and rebuild it as in the days of old, so that it may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear his name (9:12). The mountains will drip with sweet wine, and God will bring his people back from captivity. They will rebuild the ruined cities, plant vineyards and drink their wine, and he will plant them in their land, never again to be uprooted (9:13-15).

These are promises to Israel after the exile, in the words of an eighth-century prophet. They make no claim about any modern state or border.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Amos
parts.body:
At the council in Jerusalem, James quoted 9:11-12 to show that Gentiles coming to faith fulfilled what the prophets had said: ‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David’ (Acts 15:16), ‘so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name’ (Acts 15:17). James follows the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which reads the remnant of men seeking the Lord where the Hebrew speaks of possessing the remnant of Edom. The notes on chapter 9 say more about the difference.

Stephen quoted Amos 5:25-27 in his speech, to show Israel's long history of idolatry: ‘Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?’ (Acts 7:42).

These are the New Testament's own lines from Amos, and these notes draw no others. Amos's warnings were spoken to Israel by a prophet of Israel, and the New Testament never uses them to blame the Jewish people.

Read Amos's charges for what they name: particular acts of oppression and corruption, measured against Israel's covenant law. Let them land on yourself before anyone else.

Hear the questions under the book. What good is worship that leaves the poor at the gate? What does it mean that being chosen brings more accountability, not less? Who is ‘at ease in Zion’ (6:1) today, and are you among them?

Read the violent verses as Israel's own Scripture, spoken by one of its own prophets to his own people. They are warnings to take to oneself, not a verdict on anyone else's suffering. And do not skip the ending. The book that began with a lion's roar closes with vineyards replanted and a people at home.

hard.line: War crimes of the nations named and judged, though they never received the law: named here, not described.
Israel judged for selling the needy and abusing the weak: is Amos condemning wealth, or the way it was gained?
‘Only you have I known’: being chosen brings accountability, not safety.
‘If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?’: does God cause every disaster?
The cows of Bashan: a harsh image aimed at the oppression of the poor, not at women as such.
God hates Israel's feasts: does Amos reject worship altogether?
Ivory beds and bowls of wine: condemning wealth and music, or comfort that does not grieve?
Amos prays, and the LORD relents: does God change his mind?
The word against Amaziah and his family: named, not lingered on.
A famine of hearing the word of the LORD.
Israel like the Cushites to God: a chosen people among nations God also led.
The remnant of Edom in Amos, all people seeking the Lord in Acts 15.

words.line: Amos's village in Judah, south of Bethlehem, on the edge of the wilderness (1:1).
The formula that opens each judgment in chapters 1 and 2: sin piled on sin, until the last one tips the scale (1:3).
Mishpat and tsedaqah: fair dealing in court and in trade, and right relationships kept. Amos's great pair (5:7, 24).
The open space at a city's gate where elders heard cases. Justice was to be established there (5:10-15).
Bashan, east of the Jordan, had rich pastures and fat cattle. Amos's name for the wealthy women of Samaria (4:1).
Amos's call to turn from the shrines to the LORD himself (5:4, 6, 14).
The day Israel expected to be victory. Amos says it will be darkness, not light (5:18-20).
Those who may be spared. Amos holds open that God may be gracious to the remnant of Joseph (5:15).
God turning from a judgment he had spoken, in answer to Amos's prayer (7:3, 6).
A weight on a cord used to test whether a wall is straight. Israel is out of true (7:7-8).
Qayits, which sounds like qets, end: the basket that means the end has come (8:1-2).
David's house, fallen like a booth or hut, which God will rebuild (9:11).

timeline.what: The kingdom divides. Jeroboam I sets up a golden calf at Bethel (1 Kings 12), the shrine Amos speaks against.
Jeroboam II reigns in Israel and pushes its borders north and east (2 Kings 14:25).
Uzziah reigns in Judah, first beside his father Amaziah, alone from 767.
Amos preaches at Bethel, ‘two years before the earthquake’ (1:1). His ministry may have lasted a season or a year.
A strong earthquake. The guide to the kings dates traces at Hazor and other sites to about 760; the book's introduction says the link to Amos is probable but not certain.
Tiglath-pileser III comes to the throne of Assyria and turns west.
Samaria falls, about a generation after Amos (2 Kings 17). The guide to the kings, following Thiele, gives 723 or 722.
In Acts, Stephen quotes Amos 5:25-27 before his death in the 30s (Acts 7), and later James quotes 9:11-12 at the council in Jerusalem (Acts 15).

map.title: Israel, Judah and the nations of Amos 1 and 2

places.name: Bethel
places.line: The king's sanctuary, where Amos preached and Amaziah told him to go home (7:10-13). Its altars will be torn down (3:14).

places.name: Samaria
places.line: Israel's capital and its hill country, where the wealthy lay on ivory beds (3:9-15; 6:1-6). Drawn roughly, as a region; the city is not marked.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Zion, from which the LORD roars (1:2). Judah too is judged (2:4-5), and those at ease in Zion (6:1).

places.name: Beersheba
places.line: A shrine in the far south that Israelites went down to, which Amos told them not to seek (5:5).

places.name: Damascus
places.line: Capital of Aram, judged first, for threshing Gilead (1:3-5). Israel will go into exile beyond it (5:27).

places.name: Tyre
places.line: The Phoenician port that handed over whole communities and broke a covenant of brotherhood (1:9-10).

places.name: Ashdod
places.line: A Philistine city judged with Gaza (1:8), and called to witness Samaria's oppression (3:9).

places.name: Gilead
places.line: The land east of the Jordan, where Damascus and Ammon did their war crimes (1:3, 13). Drawn roughly, as a region.

teaching.mapNote: Eight places are drawn, each at a point already used on this site's maps; Samaria and Gilead roughly, as regions. Tekoa, Gilgal, Gaza, Ekron, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Carmel, Bashan, Dan, Hamath, Calneh and Gath are left off, because they are not placed in this site's records. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
